the light particle emission in the most violent collisions at 47 A MeV projectile energy is characterized by a common emission mechanism even though the deposited energies are very different.
the light particle emission in the most violent heavy-ion collisions at 47 A MeV is characterized by emission in the nucleons-nucleons frame.

the coalescence model analysis of light charged particle data from 47A Me V reactions of C-12 +Sn-116, Ne -22+Ag, Ar-40+Mo-100, and Z-64+ Y-89 indicates that the emitting source expands rapidly and reaches average densities as low as similar to 0.36rho(0) at similar to 100 fm/c, the double isotope yield ratios suggest that the temperatures of the emitting systems drop as the systems expand
In summary, our research is concerned with
a systematic study of the evolution of hot, excited nuclei produced in heavy ion collisions.
the study of the expansion of hot, dense, excited nuclear systems.
probing the early stages of the collision process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the light cluster yields are consistent with a picture of a hot and dense system which expands and cools as it emits particles and fragments.
the expansion and the temperature evolution of the system is a function of the mass of the projectile.
a common emission mechanism dominates early emission in all of these collisions and that this mechanism is characterized as emission from the nucleon-nuclon frame.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the expansion of the emitting systems is large and the excitation energy is high enough that the emitting system does not reach thermal equilibrium.

the coalescence model analysis of light charged particle emission in the reactions studied here is consistent with the picture of a system which is highly compressed and excited at the time of the initial emission of light particles.
the expansion and cooling of the emitting source is a common feature in the reactions studied, and is consistent with the predictions of QMD simulations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the expansion of the system is so large that it is necessary to take expansion effects into account in order to understand the light particle emission.
the expansion of a system is an integral part of the dynamics of the collision, and that expansion and the evolution of temperature are closely linked.
the expansion of the system, as probed by the light particle emission, is a key ingredient to understanding the evolution of the system from preequilibrium to equilibration.
